wine.name: Cloudy Bay Sauvignon Blanc
wine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, blended from many separate lots of the Wairau Valley.
wine.sites: Vineyards on the stony floor of the Wairau Valley in three of its subregions, Rapaura, Renwick and the Brancott Valley, the house's Estate and Motukawa vineyards among them.
wine.making: Eighty or more lots are tasted apart each year before the blend is chosen. Almost all of the wine is fermented cool in stainless steel tanks; a few per cent or less is fermented warmer in old French oak barriques or large oak vats, and in some years a portion with wild yeast, for texture. It is sealed under screwcap.
wine.glass: Passionfruit, gooseberry and makrut lime over white nectarine and honeydew melon, with a green lift of blackcurrant leaf; bright, cutting acidity and a stony, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, when its aromas are at their most vivid; the house says a good bottle will keep for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a tulip shaped white wine glass.

label.means: A registered New Zealand Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the wine comes from grapes grown there.
The grape named on the label makes up at least 85 per cent of the wine.
The bay into which the Wairau River runs, named by James Cook in 1770; the vineyards lie inland.

records.table: Cloudy Bay Sauvignon Blanc carried Marlborough's name abroad from its first vintage of 1985: passionfruit, gooseberry and makrut lime over a cutting acidity, almost all of it fermented cool in steel. Pour it cold, beside oysters or any dish a squeeze of lemon would suit.
records.story: The bay came first: James Cook (1728 to 1779) sailed by in February 1770 and named it Cloudy Bay, and it has since been officially named Te Koko-o-Kupe / Cloudy Bay, after its Māori name, the oyster dredge of Kupe. In 1983, by the house's account, the founding winemaker of Cape Mentelle in Margaret River tasted his first Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc and resolved to bottle what he found in it. He founded Cloudy Bay in 1985 with a young winemaker who would direct its first twenty five vintages. That first wine was made from bought Marlborough grapes in a borrowed winery in Gisborne, on the North Island, before the house built its own at Rapaura, and its passionfruit, gooseberry and cutting acidity carried Marlborough's name abroad within a decade. Pelorus, a sparkling wine, followed from the 1987 harvest, and Te Koko, a Sauvignon Blanc fermented with wild yeast and aged in barrel, from the 1996 vintage, released in 2000. Veuve Clicquot took a stake at the start of the 1990s and full ownership in 2003. For a sommelier, the vintage of 1985 is where the story of New Zealand wine abroad begins, and this is the bottle a guest is likely to name.

others.name: Te Koko
others.note: Sauvignon Blanc fermented with wild yeast and aged in oak, first made in 1996 and named for the Māori name of the bay.

others.name: Pelorus
others.note: The house's traditional method sparkling wine of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, first harvested in 1987.

traps: Cloudy Bay is a house, not a subregion: its vineyards lie inland in the Wairau Valley, and the bay itself grows no grapes.
Te Koko is barrel fermented with wild yeast, so blind it shows texture and little of the pungency of the house's classic Sauvignon Blanc.
Cloudy Bay was founded by Cape Mentelle's founding winemaker, from Margaret River in Western Australia, which candidates rarely expect.

report: The founder (Cape Mentelle's founding winemaker) and the first winemaker are living and are not named; the founder's tasting of 1983 is the house's own account, and the twenty five vintages are Greywacke's own page and a merchant's profile.

The library's style line says tank fermented; the house's notes of 2020 and 2021 have about four per cent fermented warmer in old French barriques and large oak vats and that of 2024 about one and a half per cent in large vats, with a portion on wild yeast, so the making says a few per cent or less.

The Veuve Clicquot stake is dated 1989, 1990 and 1991 by different sources, so the story says the start of the 1990s, as the Cape Mentelle record does; full ownership in 2003 rests on Wikipedia and two other accounts in the same search.

The first vintage made in Gisborne from bought fruit is Decanter's (which names the Selaks winery) and a writer's own site (which cannot be cited); no citable source gave the year of the house's own Rapaura winery, so none is given.
Te Koko's first vintage of 1996, released in 2000, rests on a Decanter timeline, LVMH's page and a sommelier school; Pelorus from the 1987 harvest on the house's history as Decanter reports it.

Cook's naming of February 1770 rests on Wikipedia and the State Library of New South Wales transcription of his journal; the year of the official dual name (2014 in Wikipedia) had no independent second source, so the story gives none.

The library's wine note for Te Koko (wild fermented and barrel aged) agrees with the house; the place Rapaura is the region record's, and the house's Sauvignon Blanc page names Rapaura as one of its three subregions.

wine.name: Brancott Estate Sauvignon Blanc
wine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, all or nearly all of the blend.
wine.sites: Vineyards across the company's holdings in Marlborough; the line began with the Brancott Vineyard, the first planting of the modern industry, set out on the Wairau Plains in 1973.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed swiftly in bag presses, and the clear juice is fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel tanks with as little exposure to air as can be, rather than in oak, so that the bottle keeps the fruit's fresh, green snap.
wine.glass: Pink grapefruit, gooseberry and honeydew melon, with passionfruit on the palate and a green note of snow pea; light and zesty, with tight, fresh acidity and a clean, quick finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, in the year or two after the vintage, while its fruit is at its freshest.
wine.serve: 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, beside shellfish, goat's cheese or a green salad.

label.means: The name Montana's wines took worldwide from 2010, after the company's first Marlborough vineyard.
A registered New Zealand Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the wine comes from grapes grown there.

records.table: Brancott Estate Sauvignon Blanc comes from the company, then called Montana, that planted modern Marlborough's first vines at Brancott in 1973 and made the region's first commercial Sauvignon Blanc in 1979. Pink grapefruit, gooseberry and passionfruit, light and zesty, it is a wine to pour young and cold.
records.story: The company began in West Auckland, where a family from Dalmatia bought land at Oratia in the Waitakere Ranges and planted a vineyard, and two sons of that family later set up Montana Wines. In the early 1970s, on the advice of a scientist of the government's research department, Montana put a deposit on farmland on the Wairau Plains of Marlborough. On 24 August 1973, before a crowd of press, politicians and business leaders, it planted the Brancott Vineyard: the day, as New Zealand's wine body tells it, that Marlborough's wine industry was born. In 1975 some of the first vines were replaced with Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, and in 1979 came the first commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, the start of the style the region is known for. Allied Domecq bought Montana in 2001, and Pernod Ricard took over Allied Domecq in 2005. From 2010 the brand took the name Brancott Estate across the world: the name of that first vineyard, and the name its wines already carried in the United States, where Montana is a state. For a sommelier, this is the bottle at the root of Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.

others.name: Brancott Estate Letter Series B Sauvignon Blanc
others.note: The house's Letter Series Sauvignon Blanc, drawn from chosen Marlborough vineyards.

traps: Brancott Estate and Montana are one company: the Montana brand took the Brancott Estate name worldwide from 2010.
Brancott's Sauvignon Blanc vines of 1975 were Marlborough's first, not New Zealand's: the grape had been planted in West Auckland in 1969.
1973 is the planting of the Brancott Vineyard and 1979 the first commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc; candidates run the two together.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1973, the planting of the Brancott Vineyard and the house's start in Marlborough, while the company behind it is older (its first West Auckland vines are 1934 in Wikipedia, Montana Wines 1961) and the brand name dates from 2010.

The family from Dalmatia is described, not named: a son's dates could not be found in two sources (New Zealand Winegrowers' feature of 2020 reads as a retrospective), and the government scientist who advised him is not named either.

The making rests on the house's entry in New Zealand Winegrowers' catalogue (bag pressed, temperature controlled steel, little oxygen) and a Decanter promotional profile (steel rather than oak); brancottestate.com refused the one fetch, so its pages were read through search, the Letter Series and Flight Song notes among them.

The first commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc of 1979 rests on Wine Marlborough, New Zealand Winegrowers and a press release of 2009 marking thirty vintages; one timeline's gold medals of 1980 and export to Britain by 1982 had no second source and are left out.

Montana's purchase of Corbans is dated 2000 by one source and 2002 by another, so it is left out, and a sale of the brand by Pernod Ricard reported for 2025 rests on one source and is too recent to tell.
The worldwide rename is 2010 in Wikipedia and Drinks International (rolled out from the 2010 vintage) and 2011 on New Zealand Winegrowers' page, so the record says from 2010.

The glass rests on the house's product page and a Wine Enthusiast review (snow pea); the ageing line is the author's judgement for a young Sauvignon Blanc without oak, and the earlier West Auckland planting of 1969 is New Zealand Winegrowers' own.

records.place: Where the Brancott and Omaka valleys meet, Southern Valleys, Marlborough

wine.name: Dog Point Section 94 Sauvignon Blanc
wine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, from one parcel of the estate.
wine.sites: A single parcel within the Dog Point Vineyard, planted in 1992 and cropped low, on the free draining silty clay loams that carry the estate's older vines; the vineyard is certified organic.
wine.making: Picked by hand and pressed as whole bunches, the juice is fermented with natural, wild yeasts in older French oak barrels, where the wine then rests for eighteen months before it is bottled without fining.
wine.glass: Flint, struck match and grapefruit pith over grilled lemon, white peach and honeydew melon, with a mealy, cashew richness; creamy and chalky in texture, with bright acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Released with more bottle age than most Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, it is open on release and keeps for several years more, growing deeper and nuttier.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, warmer than a young Sauvignon from steel; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The parcel's title in an early survey of Marlborough, made when the Hawkesbury Run was cut up.
The place named for the wild dogs, lost by shepherds, that settlers cleared from the land.
A registered New Zealand Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the wine comes from grapes grown there.

records.table: Dog Point Section 94 shows Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc's other face: one parcel planted in 1992, picked by hand, fermented with wild yeasts and kept eighteen months in older French oak. Expect flint, grapefruit pith and white peach with a creamy texture, and pour it a little warmer than usual.
records.story: As the house tells it, the place took its name from the early sheep runs: boundary dogs lost by shepherds bred into a wild pack that preyed on the flocks they were meant to guard, until settlers cleared them, and the spot became Dog Point. In the late 1970s a Marlborough couple planted their first vines there and grew grapes for others. The husband became Cloudy Bay's viticulturist, and there he worked beside one of its winemakers, who with a colleague devised Te Koko, Cloudy Bay's wild fermented, barrel aged Sauvignon Blanc. A single parcel of the vineyard was planted in 1992, and it carries its title from an early survey of Marlborough, made when the vast Hawkesbury Run was cut up: Section 94. The two couples made their first wine of their own from the 2002 vintage and launched the Dog Point label in February 2004, and Section 94 brought the barrel and the wild yeast to a parcel of their own. The vineyard was later turned over to organic growing and is certified organic. For a sommelier, Section 94 is the bottle to offer when a guest wants Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc with texture rather than snap.

others.name: Dog Point Sauvignon Blanc
others.note: The classic bottling, not barrel fermented, hand picked from eight of the house's own Wairau Valley vineyards.

others.name: Dog Point Chardonnay
others.note: Fermented in barrel with wild yeasts, as are Section 94 and the house's Pinot Noir.

traps: Section 94 is barrel fermented Sauvignon Blanc, not a Chardonnay or a blend, so blind its flint and creamy texture can mislead.
Section 94 is a single parcel planted in 1992, not a selection of barrels or a numbered cuvée of the house.
Dog Point's founders came from Cloudy Bay, but Dog Point is a separate house with its own vineyard and label.

cards.front: Dog Point Section 94: how is it fermented and aged?

cards.front: Dog Point Section 94: what does the name Section 94 record?

Cool fermentation in steel and early bottling

From a headland on Cloudy Bay shaped like a dog

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 2002, the first vintage, as the plan has it; one account has the company registered in November 2001, and the house's own page has the label launched in February 2004 with fruit of 2002.

Living people kept out: the two founding couples (the husband of one was Cloudy Bay's viticulturist, the husband of the other one of its winemakers), their son who manages the estate and its winemaker.

Section 94 as a title from the survey of the Hawkesbury Run rests on the importer's technical sheet and a New Zealand merchant's sheet; the house's own pages call it a single parcel planted in 1992, and the origin of the name Dog Point is the house's own story, told as such.
The conversion to organic growing is dated 2009 by one source only, so the story gives no year; the house calls the vineyard certified organic.
The soil is the house's general line for its older vines and white grapes (free draining silty clay loams); no source tied a soil to the Section 94 parcel alone.

The glass gathers the importer's notes of the 2015, 2017 and 2020 vintages (flint, struck match, grapefruit pith, white peach, honeydew, cashew); the ageing line is the author's judgement from the house's note that the wine comes with more bottle age than most.

Whether Section 94 was bottled from the first vintage of 2002 is not settled, so the record does not say; the place, where the Brancott and Omaka valleys meet, is the house's own and Grape Collective's.
Te Koko's devising by one of the Dog Point founders and a colleague is Cloudy Bay's own account, cited in the Cloudy Bay record.

records.place: Southern Valleys and central Wairau Plains, Marlborough

wine.name: Greywacke Wild Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, from several Marlborough vineyards.
wine.sites: Several vineyards in the Southern Valleys and on the central Wairau Plains, among them sites at Woodbourne, Renwick and Rapaura, where the soils are young alluvial deposits.
wine.making: The juice is cold settled and run into mostly old French oak barriques, where wild yeasts ferment it, the tail of the fermentation running on for months. The lees are stirred from time to time and part of the wine goes through malolactic; it leaves the barrels before the next harvest and rests some six months more on its lees before bottling.
wine.glass: Ripe peach, elderflower and lemon oil with dried mango, honeycomb and shortbread; savoury and textured, with bright acidity and a salty edge like oyster shell.
wine.ageing: Bottled about eighteen months after the harvest, it is open on release, and its savoury depth holds and grows for several years more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though it opens in the glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The name of New Zealand's most abundant bedrock, a hard grey sandstone; said GREY-wack-ee.
Sauvignon Blanc fermented in barrel by wild yeasts rather than cultured ones.
A registered New Zealand Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the wine comes from grapes grown there.

records.table: Greywacke Wild Sauvignon is the barrel fermented Marlborough Sauvignon of the house that Cloudy Bay's founding winemaker set up in 2009: wild yeasts, mostly old French barriques and long lees ageing give peach, honeycomb and a savoury, salty edge. Pour it as you would a white Burgundy.
records.story: Greywacke, said GREY-wack-ee, is the name of New Zealand's most abundant bedrock, a hard grey sandstone whose rounded stones lie in the region's riverbeds. Its founder came to Marlborough as the founding winemaker of Cloudy Bay and directed that house's first twenty five vintages from 1985, the years in which Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became known across the world. At Cloudy Bay, by that house's account, he and a colleague devised Te Koko, a Sauvignon Blanc fermented with wild yeast and aged in barrel, first made in 1996. In 2009 he and his wife set up a label of their own, buying much of its fruit from the vineyards of one of Dog Point's founding families, his former colleagues at Cloudy Bay. Wild Sauvignon carries the Te Koko thinking further: wild yeasts in mostly old French barriques, malolactic for part of the wine and long ageing on its lees, so that savour and texture stand where the usual pungency would be. The house makes a classic Sauvignon Blanc beside it, and the two poured side by side show what the barrel changes. For a sommelier, Wild Sauvignon is the proof that Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is more than one style.

others.name: Greywacke Sauvignon Blanc
others.note: The classic, tank fermented Marlborough bottling, poured beside Wild Sauvignon to show what the barrel changes.

others.name: Greywacke Pinot Noir
others.note: Mostly from the Yarrum Vineyard on the ridge between the Brancott and Ben Morven valleys.

traps: Wild Sauvignon is barrel fermented with wild yeasts, so blind its texture and muted pungency can pass for a white Bordeaux or an oaked Loire Sauvignon.
Greywacke is a house and a rock, not a subregion of Marlborough.
Greywacke was founded in 2009 by Cloudy Bay's founding winemaker; it is not a second label of Cloudy Bay.

cards.front: Greywacke: what does the name mean, and how is it said?
cards.back: New Zealand's most abundant bedrock, a hard grey sandstone; said GREY-wack-ee.

cards.back: Greywacke Wild Sauvignon, from the house of Cloudy Bay's founding winemaker.

questions.q: A guest asks why Greywacke Wild Sauvignon tastes less pungent and more savoury than most Marlborough Sauvignon. Which reason fits?
opts: Wild yeasts in old barrels, malolactic and long lees ageing
Grapes from the cool, high Awatere Valley alone
Fermentation in new American oak with cultured yeast
A blend with Chardonnay from the Southern Valleys
questions.exp: The house ferments with wild yeasts in mostly old French barriques, puts part of the wine through malolactic and keeps it long on lees; the cooler Awatere gives a greener wine, not a savoury one.

opts: Cloudy Bay
Dog Point Vineyard
Brancott Estate
Fromm Winery

Cloudy Bay: 40 Years in the Making

report: founded keeps the library's 2009, the house's own year; the founder, his wife and the house's winemaker are living and are not named, and the library's holdings line names the founder, which the record here does not.

That much of the fruit comes from one Dog Point family's vineyards rests on two merchants' accounts (about three quarters, and about seventy per cent); one of them, and a further account that the wines are made in Dog Point's winery, sit at addresses that name the founder and cannot be cited, so the winery is left out.
The making and the sites rest on the house's notes of the 2023 and 2024 vintages; the malolactic share and the lees time vary by year, so the record says part of the wine and some six months.

That the couple registered the name in the early 1990s, inspired by a river stone, rests on one merchant's interview and is left out; the rounded stones in the riverbeds rest on the Marlborough Express and the house's bedrock line.
The Te Koko beat (devised by the founder and a colleague) is Cloudy Bay's own account, and the twenty five vintages are the house's own page and a merchant's profile.
The ageing line is the author's judgement from the house's bottling date, about eighteen months after the harvest; the Pinot Noir's Yarrum Vineyard is the house's own.

wine.name: Fromm Clayvin Vineyard Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The Clayvin Vineyard, closely planted on north facing slopes at the end of the Brancott Valley, on the heavy clay that gives it its name, and grown organically.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented with indigenous yeasts, the wine is matured in seasoned French oak barriques for well over a year and bottled without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Wild raspberry, blackberry and dried strawberry with orange peel, sandalwood and a forest floor note; firm, sappy tannin, fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young; the house's own drinking windows start about five years after the vintage, and a good year keeps for fifteen.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment, since it is unfiltered; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The hillside vineyard at the end of the Brancott Valley, named for its clay soil.
The grape named on the label makes up at least 85 per cent of the wine.
A registered New Zealand Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the wine comes from grapes grown there.

records.table: Fromm Clayvin Vineyard Pinot Noir comes from a Swiss founded house that made red wine its focus in Sauvignon country. Grown organically on the clay slopes of the Brancott Valley and bottled unfined and unfiltered, it brings wild raspberry, orange peel and sappy tannin; give it five years.
records.story: The Fromm family makes wine at Malans in Graubünden, in eastern Switzerland, and in the late 1980s a winegrower of that family and a fellow Swiss winemaker resolved to make wine in Marlborough. In 1992, by the house's account, Fromm Winery began with its first harvest, and its founding vineyard was planted that year; in a region turning to Sauvignon Blanc, the house made red grapes its focus, Pinot Noir, Syrah and Malbec. In the early 1990s a viticulturist and his wife planted Clayvin, closely spaced on north facing clay slopes at the end of the Brancott Valley, a vineyard often called Marlborough's first commercial hillside planting, and in 1998 they sold it to Fromm. Its Pinot Noir, grown organically, fermented with indigenous yeasts and bottled unfined and unfiltered, became the wine by which the house is known. The founding family returned to Switzerland in 2008, and the estate passed to Swiss partners. In 2015, after a long lease, the Marlborough house of Giesen bought the vineyard, and Fromm has gone on making its Clayvin wines from the site. For a sommelier, Clayvin shows what Marlborough's clay hillsides can give Pinot Noir: grip and depth from a region better known for Sauvignon Blanc.

others.name: Fromm Syrah
others.note: The house's Syrah, co-fermented with Viognier, one of the red grapes it made its focus.

others.name: Fromm Chardonnay Clayvin Vineyard
others.note: Chardonnay from the same clay slopes of the Brancott Valley.

traps: Clayvin is a vineyard, not a subregion: it lies at the end of the Brancott Valley, one of Marlborough's Southern Valleys.
Giesen also bottles wines named Clayvin from the same vineyard, so a guest must read the house as well as the site.
Fromm Winery is a Marlborough house with Swiss roots, not the Fromm family's own estate at Malans in Switzerland.

Cultured yeasts, new American oak, sterile filtration
Carbonic maceration in steel, bottled within months
Fermented in amphora and aged under flor
questions.exp: The house ferments with indigenous yeasts, matures the wine in seasoned French barriques and bottles it unfined and unfiltered; it is no carbonic red bottled within months.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1992, the year of the first harvest and of the founding vineyard by the house's own pages, and the founders met in the late 1980s; the return to Switzerland in 2008 is the house's and two secondary accounts.
Living people kept out: the Swiss founder and his wife, the founding winemaker, the couple who planted Clayvin and the Swiss partners.

Clayvin's planting is 1991 in the Marlborough Express and one Giesen page and 1992 and 1993 on other Giesen pages, so the story says the early 1990s; the sale to Fromm in 1998 rests on the Marlborough Express and Winepilot, and Giesen's purchase of 2015 after a long lease on Giesen's own history and Winepilot.

The house's own pages carry a 2022 Clayvin Vineyard Pinot Noir and a 2020 Clayvin Chardonnay, so it has gone on bottling the site after 2015; on what terms it takes the fruit is not known and the record does not say.

The making rests on the house's 2022 page and the reviews it reprints (hand picked, indigenous yeasts, French barriques, unfined and unfiltered, sixteen months in seasoned barrels in 2022), so the record says well over a year.

The ageing reads the house's drinking windows (from 2027 for the 2022, 2020 to 2030 for the 2015); the red focus on Pinot Noir, Syrah and Malbec is the house's vineyard page and a Marlborough tour guide.
Left out: the family's winemaking at Malans since 1866 (one tourism page), the Malbec vines called the region's oldest (one source), and a sale of the estate reported in 2025, too recent to tell.
The place is the flagship's valley; the winery and cellar door stand at Fairhall near Blenheim by New Zealand Winegrowers' listing, which could not be cited within five sources.
